title: Ari Emanuel on Outrunning ‘Entourage,’ the Art of the Phone Call and the Stolen Commission that Still Hurts

body:
The Thomas Guide Is a map that painstakingly details how to navigate Los Angeles by car. It’s a spiral-bound relic that almost none of your junior executives remember. Your assistant thinks it’s a ranking of pale British heartthrobs. Your intern will stare at you, unblinkingly and for minutes, if you even ask.

	But Ari Emanuel has used it as a kind of blueprint to build an empire. The familiar byways of Century City, the lofty heights of the Bird Streets, the humble beginnings south of Olympic Boulevard — he’s traveled all of them. The guide is also one of the ways the super agent anchors “Roll the Calls,” a memoir of the TKO chief executive and WME Group executive chairman’s rage-fueled rise to the top of show business that hits shelves this week.
	

	As the book rolls out, coupled with upcoming live events including in Los Angeles, Variety scored 18 (anger-free!) minutes with Emanuel to discuss his tome and outlook on the business today. Here he dissects the art of the phone call, the stolen commission that still keeps him up at night and the unholy rise of the text message.

	
		Why was this the right time to jump in and tell your life story?	

	Well, it’s been a hell of a ride. I know [this memoir] was shocking to people, because most of my life I’ve just been a voice for clients. This book is really for two [groups] of people. First, the parents that come to me with anxiety having to raise kids with ADHD and dyslexia — and how to find a way to deal with that. Looking back at it, my mom and dad let me go through it and struggle while still making sure I had all the tools. It was incredible because it taught me to be a free thinker. That’s helped me in business and helped me with the people in my life. The other [group] — I wrote this book as my own version of the Thomas Guide, to surviving [the industry]. To succeed, you have to realize how hard it is. You have to be relentless, consistent, have emotional endurance. And it doesn’t come quickly. I didn’t have a “Plan B.” It was only “Plan A.” I wanted to show that sacrifice through stories and hopefully give other people a road map to get there.
	
	
		Have you realized that in recent years many agents don’t “roll calls” anymore?	

	I’ll tell my assistants — not my current two, because they’ve gotten it — but I ask them to call [someone] and I’ll follow up and ask if they talked to them. The assistants will say, “Well, I texted.” But that’s not what I asked for. I asked you to call. I understand that texts and DMs are how we have the conversation now, but I like the personal [nature] of a phone call. I’ll also have my assistant call back after 15-20 minutes. They’ll say, “We just left word.” Call again!
	
		Do you text?	

	I’m a one-word texter. Maybe two words.
	
		I bet.	

	You can also just leave a voice note now.
	
		You know people can keep those files, right? What do you think the talent agencies look like in 10 years?	

	The overall content business — from live sports to live events, movies, TV, podcasts, social, concerts, books, lectures — it’s all going to expand. I also think we’ll see more production … and costs will come down because of AI. The creators will keep making small movies that make a lot of money [like “Obsession”]. You’re going to start seeing a lot of new development around that. Steve Jobs [once spoke about] a study about humans. That they were the slowest-moving mammals until the invention of the bicycle, then became the fastest. So, whatever [Hollywood looks like in the future], we’ll still need legs to pedal those bikes.
	
		It seems like the agencies are under increased pressure to consolidate, like the rest of Hollywood. Is that a good thing?	

	I have no idea. There will probably need to be more consolidation. But remember — Charlie Bludhorn took over Paramount all those years ago and wrote off the movie business. Then, out of nowhere, they made “The Godfather” and “Chinatown.” Barry Diller announces five years ago that the movie business is dead, then he tries to buy Paramount. When I started in the business, they said packaging was over. They said half hours were dead. They said dramas were over. This is a business that has gone on for over 100 years and it’s not going anywhere. I haven’t thought through what that means for talent agencies, but they’re going to be around. People are talented. They’re going to have to be represented.
	
	
		There are many revelations in “Roll the Calls,” but something I can’t get over: You write that, in the mid-‘90s, you put the “architecture” together for CJ Entertainment to buy a minority investment in the startup DreamWorks. You said Jeff Berg, the head of ICM Partners at the time, took that entire commission for himself.	

	I give him credit. He owned the company. Jeff Berg took the money. [So I said], “Yeah, great. See you later. I’ll make my own.”
	
		How much would you have cleared for that transaction?	

	I don’t know how much he made. But he paid for a house, probably. I didn’t own a house at that point, I had a duplex.
	
		About 10-15 years ago, I think a lot of people in your life would’ve said you’ll never outrun Ari Gold — Jeremy Piven’s caricature of you from “Entourage.” But I’m not sure. I think you may have.	

	You know, my wife has helped. My new marriage, and the work I’ve done on myself has helped. Looking back, it was a great ride but I don’t want to be that guy anymore.
	
		So you’re not going to help reboot “Entourage’ any time soon?	

	No, definitely not.
	
		Talk to me about the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger and where we stand today.	

	I’m sitting here watching CNBC on mute. I’ve stated this publicly in op-eds, but we’ve had six bad years between COVID and the strikes. Based on all the indications from people in distribution, in film, in the cable [sector] – it seems that this isn’t about anything other than CNN and politics. Let’s move on from that and make a deal.

schema.headline: Ari Emanuel on Outrunning ‘Entourage,’ the Art of the Phone Call and the Stolen Commission that Still Hurts

title: Spike Lee, Bowen Yang, Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco and Chance the Rapper Front J.Crew’s 40th Anniversary Barn Jacket Campaign

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	J.Crew is celebrating 40 years of its signature Barn Jacket with a sprawling new campaign featuring everyone from Spike Lee and Bowen Yang to Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco, Chance the Rapper and Scottie Pippen.

	Unveiled Tuesday, the campaign brings together 160 people photographed across New York City, Los Angeles, Austin, Boston and Chicago, marking what J.Crew calls its most ambitious portrait project to date. The lineup spans actors, musicians, athletes, designers, artists and local personalities, with Jenny Slate, Hari Nef, Vince Staples, Ryan Beatty, Owen Thiele, Aly Raisman and Chloe East also among the familiar faces modeling the brand staple.


	Photographer Robert Nethery shot the cast in a stripped-down portrait style, with each subject putting their own spin on the Barn Jacket. Accompanying films bring members of the group together to discuss personal style, their respective cities and the jacket’s staying power.



	

	





	

	



	“The scale of this campaign is extraordinary, but its power comes from the individuality within it,” J.Crew chief marketing officer Julia Collier said in a statement. “We brought together 160 people across five cities to show how one iconic piece can take on an entirely different life through every person who wears it.”

	First introduced by J.Crew in 1986, the Barn Jacket has become one of the retailer’s most recognizable pieces, borrowing from traditional workwear with its boxy silhouette, utility-minded construction and easy layering appeal.

	For its anniversary, J.Crew is also introducing a new 2026 version of the jacket with updated proportions. The wider anniversary collection comprises 29 styles across women’s, men’s and kids offerings, ranging from the familiar cotton canvas construction to new fabrics, finishes and embellished takes.


	“The Barn Jacket has always had an ease and utility that make it incredibly versatile,” said Olympia Gayot, J.Crew’s creative director of women’s and kids. “The shape is timeless, but it takes on a completely different personality depending on who is wearing it and how they style it.” Gayot added that the piece can skew “polished, rugged, feminine, oversized, familiar or unexpected,” pointing to that adaptability as a reason it has remained a mainstay in J.Crew’s assortment for four decades.

	The Barn Jacket campaign builds on J.Crew’s recent effort to reintroduce archival staples to a new generation. The brand launched its “Next Rollneck Generation” last fall and more recently an updated version of its rollneck sweater fronted by Emma Chamberlain.

	Shop J. Crew‘s signature barn jacket here.

body:
In line with mega-mergers that have come before, the impending marriage of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery will lead to a media company packed with assets. What differentiates this deal — which is now in the clear to move forward — from others is the sheer amount of brands and intellectual property in play.

	David Ellison’s newly merged entity will house a mountain of content, given that Paramount (which was acquired last year by Skydance Media) and Warner Bros. (which was bought by Discovery) have already doubled up their respective lineups of TV shows, movies, streamers and networks. Ellison told employees Monday he expects the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close in about two weeks following the settlement of the 12-state antitrust lawsuit that sought to block the deal.
	

	The programming list alone is a monster to contend with, spanning Harry Potter (which is about to be revived with a new HBO series) and “Game of Thrones” at Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount’s “Yellowstone” universe and Nickelodeon empire. But then there are also the streaming services (HBO Max and Paramount+), linear networks (e.g., HGTV and CBS), news organizations (CNN and CBS News) and other entities, like video game studios, to account for.

title: Nancy Meyers’ Daughter Just Launched a Target Home Collection That Looks Straight Out of One of Her Mom’s Movies
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Nancy Mey
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Nancy Meyers has spent decades making audiences covet the kitchens, living rooms and impossibly cozy interiors in her movies. Now, her daughter is making that aesthetic a little easier to bring home.

	Target has teamed with Annie Meyers-Shyer, the author and creator behind @ThisOakHouse, for a new home collection under its Threshold label, featuring vintage-inspired decor. The lineup includes throw pillows, ceramic vases, hurricane candle holders, faux greenery, woven accents and a knit throw, with prices starting at $25. The collection launched Sept. 13 in select Target stores and online.


		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										LIMITED-EDITION						

					Threshold – A Collection with @ThisOakHouse		

		
	

	The collaboration takes inspiration from Meyers-Shyer’s affinity for antiques, natural materials and interiors that look as though they’ve been assembled over time rather than bought all at once. It arrives as Target continues to refresh its longtime Threshold home brand with more distinctive designs and higher-end details at accessible price points.

	“I really believe beautiful things should be part of everyday living,” Meyers-Shyer said of the collection. “Good design shouldn’t depend on price point, and everyone deserves to live with things they find beautiful.”

	Among her favorite pieces are the collection’s glass hurricanes, which she says she uses throughout her own home year-round, along with lumbar pillows inspired by a style she had been unable to find for herself and a knit throw designed to balance coziness with a more polished look.

	The designer’s approach is decidedly anti-showroom. For Meyers-Shyer, a home gets its character from books, family photos, travel souvenirs and other personal objects — and the nicer pieces shouldn’t be kept tucked away for special occasions.


	“A home should feel lived in, not staged,” she said.

	The collaboration is also part of a broader evolution for Threshold in 2026. Mara Sirhal, Target’s senior vice president of merchandising for home, said the retailer is sharpening the brand’s aesthetic with “more distinctive design, elevated details and incredible value,” with additional designer collections still to come.

title: ‘Digger’ First Reactions Split Over Tom Cruise’s ‘Baffling,’ ‘Unpleasant’ and ‘Brave’ New Movie: ‘The Divide on This Is Going to Be Wide’
description: Tom Cruise‘s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy.
body:
Tom Cruise‘s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy. The latest directorial effort from “Birdman” and “The Revenant” Oscar winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is being called everything from “baffling” to “unpleasant” to “fascinating stuff.” Most film journalists seem to agree on one thing: “Digger” is like nothing you’re expecting.

	“This is Tom Cruise’s most dynamic and interesting role in years,” writes Next Best Picture founder Matt Neglia. “It provides him plenty of space to preach to the back row but not enough to dig deeper and deliver a performance that could’ve had far more power and nuance had Alejandro González Iñárritu’s ambitious narrative not been so imbalanced in favor of its zany but empty theatrics.”Variety’s awards pundit Clayton Davis adds: “I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work, and the production design and cinematography are impressive. In the end, not all the dots connect, and I wish the film leaned harder into the absurdity and satire it kept reaching for. Shocker! The divide on this one is going to be wide.”
	

	Awards Radar’s Joey Magidson called the movie a “mess,” claiming that “not a whole lot works here” and “this wasn’t enjoyable,” while critic Edward Douglas added: “I cannot say that ‘Digger’ is very good, although I could tell what Iñarritu and Cruise were going for… I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore.” A similar opinion was shared by journalist Mike Ryan, who called the movie “unpleasant.”
	

	IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill was more positive, writing the movie “not only showcases Tom Cruise’s best performance since ‘Magnolia,’ it’s one of the most visually inventive, conceptually audacious, and unpredictable studio movies ever made. Takes so many bold aesthetic swings it makes ‘Bardo’ look like an episode of ‘The Golden Girls.'”

	Anne Thompson of IndieWire was also high on the movie, calling it “a brave and gorgeous art film that will not score with mainstream audiences but will play best for the Academy, especially crafts and actors.”

	“Digger” stars Cruise as Digger Rockwell, a wealthy tycoon who must save the world when one of his oil rigs malfunctions and causes an environmental catastrophe across the planet. The film’s supporting cast includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons.

	For Cruise, “Digger” notably marks his return to adult-oriented drama after more than a decade playing action movie heroes. In the last 10 years, Cruise’s only non-action movie is the 2017 crime comedy “American Made.” One would have to go back 20 years to add more non-action movies to Cruise’s roster, such as the musical “Rock of Ages,” the political drama “Lions for Lambs,” the comedy “Tropic Thunder” and the historical thriller “Valkyrie.” Cruise’s return to more dramatic fare has raised the eyebrows of Oscar pundits since “Digger” was announced a few years ago, but the wildly divisive reactions to “Digger” may upend his expected awards campaign.

	Prior to the film’s release, much of the buzz surrounding “Digger” has related to Cruise’s wild transformation into the title role. The actor appears under heavy makeup and prosthetics that originally took six hours to apply. Cruise worked with the movie’s makeup department to get the transformation time down to an hour. 

	“I had a guy there with a stopwatch and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,’” Cruise said on the “New Heights” podcast. “They were like, ‘No, I’m not doing that, it will never happen.’ I’m like, ‘OK, first of all, if you say no, you can’t do it, you will never get there. So can we agree that we’ll maybe make it a little less?’ So with each piece that was going on, it was timed and then we’d drill and practice.”
	

	“Digger” opens in theaters Oct. 1 from Warner Bros. Check out first reactions in the posts below.

title: College Sports Betting Series ‘Knockouts’ in the Works at Paramount TV Studios, Skydance Sports From Clara Nevins, Harper Oreck(EXCLUSIVE)
description: In a competitive situation, Paramount Television Studios and Skydance Sports have landed the spec script “Knockouts” from writers Clara Nevins and H
body:
In a competitive situation, Paramount Television Studios and Skydance Sports have landed the spec script “Knockouts” from writers Clara Nevins and Harper Oreck, Variety has learned exclusively. 

	Per the official logline, the show is “set against the glossy world of SEC sports and Southern sorority life, where four girls in a bottom-tier sorority use their insider knowledge to build an illegal sports betting ring out of their basement.” 
	

	Both Nevins and Oreck are executive producers in addition to writing. Marty Bowen, Wyck Godfrey, and James Seidman will executive produce via Temple Hill. Paramount TV Studios and Skydance Sports will co-produce.


	Nevins and Oreck graduated from Harvard in 2023, where they originally met and started writing together. Nevins was previously an assistant at Counterpart Studios, while Oreck recently completed a master’s degree in gender studies at the University of Cambridge. They previously worked together on the short film “Tank Top.”

	They are repped by UTA and Kaplan Perrone. Temple Hill is repped by UTA. 

	Sports betting has become the focus of renewed scrutiny in recent years with the launch of numerous betting apps that have given people the ability to wager as much as they want right from their phones. There was a case earlier this year in which a group of gamblers were charged with bribing college basketball players in attempts to affect the outcomes of the NCAA March Madness tournament from 2023-2025. There have also been numerous accusations of anonymous accounts wagering on seemingly insider information in an effort win untold amounts of money.

title: ‘Compound’ Uses Security Camera Footage to Show the Violent Downfall of an Off-the-Grid Family, Reflecting America’s Increasing Surveillance State Paranoia
description: Sometimes films come out at a time that lines up eerily well with real life. As Americans debate the ethics of the nearly ubiquitous Flock cameras t
body:
Sometimes films come out at a time that lines up eerily well with real life. As Americans debate the ethics of the nearly ubiquitous Flock cameras that are being placed in neighborhoods all throughout the nation, with only vague information made available about how they will help police, citizens of all political stripes are worried about this increased monitoring.

	That real-life backdrop feeds squarely into the world of “Compound,” a thriller where privacy and surveillance push a community to the brink. In the film, a paranoid family living off the grid constantly records their remote property via a series of interconnected cameras. Things get dire and violent as the outside world begins threatening the solitude of the well-armed family. The end result is a feature stitched together from the footage.
	

	“Building this world of the Williams compound, led by Sarah Williams, this veteran who is paranoid, it would make sense that she would install all these cameras across her property where she’s trying to teach her kids her lifestyle,” director and cowriter James Mulcahy says. “So it was a surveillance camera movie first, tied to this authenticity, tied to family. For me, the best type of horror movie is a movie that’s about something a little bit more. Finding these themes of paranoia and familial bonds really came to life once we started playing around on the property and really developing the characters and what we could do with the cameras.”

	“Compound,” which began screening as part of this year’s TIFF marketplace, was shot on location at a Texas cabin using real security cameras rigged around the property. While it was a way to keep the budget down, it called for a deconstruction of how the narrative would be shot. In order to add realism, Mulcahy, who wrote the film with Max Perkins, created a system of filming he called “The Immersive World Approach.”
	

	“It’s a hot set everywhere,” he says. “For one scene, there might be six or seven cameras rolling, capturing it from different vantage points. The actors really have to live in the scene. There might be a few pages of script, but we’re starting before those pages and we’re going after those pages. Even when they think they are done, they still have to stay in character because another camera might be catching them. In post, it became a fun game to construct how it would be told because we had so many options.”

	One of the toughest parts of this approach was that the actors themselves were somewhat isolated, making it challenging to relay new ideas or tweaks to them.

	“We’re in a basic control room and trying to watch six or seven different angles,” Mulcahy says. “Giving performance notes was kind of a relay game through walkies and things like that. But that’s the nature of the shoot. You’re kind of removed from the action at certain points, and we were too when we were directing and watching.”

	While more traditional filmmakers might balk at the approach, the “Compound” team embraced the quirkiness.

	“I love creativity within constraint,” Mulcahy says. “We did a number of workshops and choreography of the action and the stunts. We built them around the frame early. ‘How do we make this cool in edit?’ Maybe that’s the normal question, but for us, it was how to make this cool practically, live in this frame that we can’t change. That became a lot of fun, and it became kind of a test. I think it forces you to be more creative sometimes and there’s a better result.”

	Despite being so unconventional, Mulcahy is optimistic that audiences in pursuit of dynamic new storytelling will find “Compound.”

	“People say they want something that’s very fresh and original, and we tried to do something that felt like nothing else, both in the way it’s consumed and also in the way it’s made,” he says. “Hopefully, people will respond to that.”

	As we wrap our conversation, I quip that with the ubiquity of Flock cameras, Mulcahy could film a spiritual sequel in his native New Jersey.

	“Seriously … that’s no joke,” he says. “People are really thinking about the cameras around them in a way they haven’t before. It’s a little by accident that this kind of movie is happening at this moment. But it’s this idea of, ‘When does paranoia about a thing manifest the thing?’ It’s at the core of the story, and I think we’re dealing with a lot of that in society right now.”

schema.headline: ‘Compound’ Uses Security Camera Footage to Show the Violent Downfall of an Off-the-Grid Family, Reflecting America’s Increasing Surveillance State Paranoia

title: Jake Paul’s Betting App Slams HBO After Cease and Desist Letter Sent Over ‘Entourage’ Reunion Ad: HBO ‘Does Not Own Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Jake Paul’s gambling app Betr has fired back at HBO after the cabler sent a cease-and-desist letter over an ad reuniting “Entourage” stars Jeremy Pi
body:
Jake Paul’s gambling app Betr has fired back at HBO after the cabler sent a cease-and-desist letter over an ad reuniting “Entourage” stars Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier. 

	In the letter, HBO threatened legal action if the commercial was not taken down, arguing that the three-minute spot infringes on its intellectual property and was made without its consent. “Everything about the Infringing Advertisement, from its setting, to the actors’ clothing, dialogue, and manner of speech, is evocative, if not duplicative, of ‘Entourage,'” read the letter, which claims Betr intended to “evoke ‘Entourage’ and to exploit the show’s popularity” for its own commercial purposes.
	

	In response to the cease and desist, Betr issued a statement to Variety that cites previous copyright-infringement lawsuits filed against HBO in relation to “Ballers” and “Six Feet Under,” both of which HBO won.


	“HBO owns ‘Entourage.’ It does not own Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier. When HBO was sued over ‘Ballers’ and ‘Six Feet Under,’ it told the courts that Miami parties, celebrity lifestyles, and fast-talking characters belong to everyone. It won that argument. Now that it is the one complaining, those same elements have become HBO’s sole and exclusive property. HBO cannot have it both ways, and it should not expect anyone to take its letter seriously when it is arguing against itself.”

	Referencing the “Entourage” creator’s public criticisms of the ad, the Betr statement continues, “Doug Ellin’s own comment that it was ‘pretty damn obvious’ he did not write the commercial confirms what everyone already knew: this is a Betr ad, made by Betr, with two actors playing themselves. We are proud of this campaign, and we stand with Jeremy and Adrian and their right to their own names, faces, and voices. Nobody needs HBO’s permission to hire two great actors.”
	

	In the Betr ad, Piven and Grenier are not explicitly reprising their “Entourage” roles of agent Ari Gold and movie star Vincent Chase. However, HBO and “Entourage” creator Ellin have argued that, based on the performances and dialogue, the actors are essentially playing the same characters. (The ad sees Piven snaking his way through a star-studded mansion party to find Grenier on a yacht, where he pitches him a new movie.)

	Betr has countered this argument by asserting that the ad contains no mention of “Entourage” and does not use its character names, footage, dialogue or music. “Viewers who know ‘Entourage’ will recognize the two actors and enjoy the nod to their shared history,” reads the letter, obtained by Variety. “Betr does not deny that association. It is part of the appeal of casting two actors with a history together. Recognition is not reproduction.”

	The letter notes that in a 2016 lawsuit, HBO argued that “Miami, lavish lifestyles, professional athletes, parties, boats, VIP settings, flashy cars, and a fast-paced, party-driven mood” were not “protectable expression.” Per Betr’s attorneys, “What HBO called stock as a defendant it calls ‘creative expression’ as a plaintiff.”

	Betr also argues that the press coverage surrounding the Piven-Grenier ad, as well as Ellin’s own comments (the series creator called it a “cheap, shitty imitation”), have made it clear to audiences that the commercial is not connected to “Entourage.”

	Betr has declined HBO’s demands to take down the ad, while asking the company to “please identify” the “specific protectable expression from ‘Entourage'” that was allegedly reproduced, as well as evidence that “consumers were confused about who produced or sponsored” the commercial.

	Summarizing its arguments, the letter concludes, in part, “HBO owns ‘Entourage.’ It does not own the men who made it.”

schema.headline: Jake Paul’s Betting App Slams HBO After Cease and Desist Letter Sent Over ‘Entourage’ Reunion Ad: HBO ‘Does Not Own Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘60 Minutes’ Notches Ratings Gain Over Last Year, but Cedes Viewers From Season Premiere
description: CBS News’ “60 Minutes” shed some of the viewers it snared during its much-anticipated Season 59 debut as it grappled with the effects of CBS’ footba
body:
CBS News’ “60 Minutes” shed some of the viewers it snared during its much-anticipated Season 59 debut as it grappled with the effects of CBS’ football programming on its audience, even as it notched a gain in audience compared to its year-earlier performance.

	The audience for the second telecast of the venerable newsmagazine rose 5% over last season’s second-week telecast, according to data from Nielsen, rising to nearly 6.77 million, compared with nearly 6.46 million a year ago. Viewership among people between 25 and 54, the demographic desired most by advertisers in news programming, rose 18%, to 1.08 million, compared with 917,000 last year. CBS News was also impressed by social views for the episode, which totaled 179.2 million, compared with 116.7 million for the prior week  — a new record for the show.
	

	Nonetheless, linear viewership for the show is down compared to the prior week, when CBS News enjoyed a national NFL lead-in that helped boost the initial audience for the program.


	And the numbers are below last season’s average. The overall audience for “60 Minutes” last season was 8.16 million, according to Nielsen, and 1.32 million in the 25-to-54 demographic.

	CBS News remains under intense pressure to demonstrate stability at the program, which was overhauled in chaotic fashion at the end of last season, despite mustering a notable 9% uptick in overall viewership. Bari Weiss, CBS News’ editor in chief, ousted Tanya Simon, an executive producer with years of history working at the show, in favor of Nick Bilton, a journalist and screenwriter with less formal TV experience. Also pushed out were correspondents Scott Pelley, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi. Anderson Cooper left of his own volition following the end of his contract. Their replacements, which include Ross Douthat and contributors like Ariel Levy and Sebastian Junger, have top-shelf backgrounds, but also little experience working on a weekly TV program that emphsizes long-form enterprise journalism.
	

	Sunday’s “60 Minutes” featured a big “get” that would have raised eyebrows at a true-crime series like NBC News’ “Dateline” or ABC News’ “20/20,” or even on one of the national morning-news programs. New correspondent Ross Douthat interviewed Patrick Clancy, former husband to Lindsay Clancy when she strangled their three children and claimed mental illness as a factor. The interview led Sunday’s show and delved into whether Patrick Clancy forgave his ex-wife, and allowed him to introduce his new spouse. Some of those elements came at the expense of more investigative work into the problems the medical industry has dealing with treating post-partum depression. Other segments featured Jon Wertheim on the trail of a long-missing racehorse and Norah O’Donnell examining sentiment toward the construction of data centers in rural areas of the nation.

	The audience for the first telecast of the season fell 21% from last year’s season kick off, according to data from Nielsen, a drop of more than 2 million viewers — resulting in an audience of about 7.94 million, compared with nearly 10.02 million from last year’s open. Meanwhile, viewers between the ages of 25 and 54 fell 33% from year-ago figures, according to Nielsen, to about 1.58 million, compared to 2.36 million for last year’s season premiere. CBS’ NFL telecast leading into the season premiere drew a smaller audience than it did last year.

title: ‘Wonder Woman’ Director Patty Jenkins Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Is ‘Such Chaos’: ‘The Studio System Is in Bad Shape’
description: Patty Jenkins, Halle Berry, Regina King, Misty Copeland and others gathered at downtown Manhattan’s Locanda Verde on Tuesday morning for Tribeca and
body:
Patty Jenkins, Halle Berry, Regina King, Misty Copeland and others gathered at downtown Manhattan’s Locanda Verde on Tuesday morning for Tribeca and Chanel’s Through Her Lens luncheon. The timing was notable for an event centered on emerging filmmakers, coming just 24 hours after news that the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal is essentially complete — a consolidation that many in Hollywood fear could have profoundly negative effects on the industry.
	

	“I didn’t even look at it, frankly. I’ve been tuning all of that out,” “Wonder Woman” director Patty Jenkins, who has a longstanding relationship with Warner Bros., tells Variety of the news. “It’s such chaos. I think the studio system is in such bad shape that I’m kind of tuning it out.”


	Still, Jenkins remains optimistic about the industry’s future. Asked whether she would make a film with Warner Bros. under Ellison’s leadership, she says, “You never know.”

	“I never say no to anything because so many people have different projects,” she continues. “Something may come along, and they’ve been making some great films, and who knows.”

	Despite the turmoil within the studio system, Jenkins believes emerging filmmakers face fewer barriers than they did when she was starting out. She points to films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession” as encouraging proof that talented directors can make films on shoestring budgets — and find box office success.

	“People are able to make their own films and it’s a game-changer,” she says. “I see it coming and I’m so excited about it — the democratization of being able to get your films to your audiences.”
	

	Tribeca boss Jane Rosenthal, who co-founded Tribeca and Chanel’s Through Her Lens program 11 years ago, takes a somewhat different view, arguing that young filmmakers actually face more obstacles than when she started out. “The business is really kind of a mess,” she says, noting that streaming has contributed to an uptick in the number of films being made. Still, she adds, “Who knows what this merger is gonna do.”

	One potential silver lining of the merger, according to Rosenthal, is that it could create an opening for new models of independent film distribution. “You see what AMC is doing, let’s see what that really means,” she says, referring to the indie distribution venture announced by the country’s largest theater chain last month.

	That hopeful, solution-oriented attitude carried throughout the event, which kicked off this year’s Through Her Lens program. The initiative brings together five filmmaking teams for workshops, one-on-one mentorship and industry conversations before culminating in a live pitch to a jury. One team will receive full financing to produce its short film with support from Tribeca Studios, while the remaining four will receive development grants.

	Berry, King and Meg Ryan were announced as this year’s jury members alongside cinematographer Autumn Durald Arkapaw (“Sinners”) and “Sterling Point” actress Ella Rubin.

	Emmy Rossum, who attended Tuesday morning to support the initiative, says she “just wants the best people to tell stories” — and, she adds, “to be seen by lots of people in theaters and on streaming.”

description:

                          Doctor Was Giving Him Ketamine ...
body:
Presley Gerber
                          Doctor Was Giving Him Ketamine ...
                          Despite Being A Persistent Issue For Him
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 22, 2026
                            11:03 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 22, 2026
                                1:12 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Presley Gerber's doctor was prescribing him ketamine despite his known issues with the substance ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            People who were in regular contact with Presley and who have direct knowledge tell TMZ ... a doctor was giving him ketamine despite knowing about his drug addiction issues. Ketamine can be used to treat drug addiction, though that's not its FDA-approved intention.
      
    
            Ketamine was a regular problem for Presley, we're told ... and close friends are angry the doctor prescribed the substance to him -- and they think the doc should be prosecuted.
      

            To be clear ... we still don't know what drugs might have been in Presley's system when he died -- just that Presley opened up about his issues with ketamine to close friends before he passed away.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Presley's situation sounds eerily similar to Matthew Perry's before his 2023 death. Remember, Matthew -- who dealt with drug addiction for years -- was prescribed ketamine for depression and anxiety.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Mathew, however, began to get ketamine from other sources ... specifically the "Ketamine Queen" Jasveen Sangha, who was sentenced to 15 years in prison for her role in Perry's death.
      
    
            We broke the story ... Presley died in a rehab facility on Sunday. He is believed to have died from an overdose, but the official cause of death is still pending.
      
    
            Sources who had contact with Presley in his final few hours told us he looked like he was under the influence at the rehab center. The source of the alleged drugs is still being investigated ... and police have even interviewed other rehab patients.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            In the months before his death, Presley was trying alternative treatments for addiction ... including ibogaine -- a psychoactive substance which some believe opens up new neural pathways and can help people addicted to drugs.
      
    
            Presley's autopsy is complete ... and now we'll just have to wait for the results.

title: Tyra Banks Says Video Shows 'ANTM' Netflix Documentary Twisted Her Words
description:
Tyra Banks vs. Netflix
                          Videos Show What 'ANTM' Doc Left Out!!!
body:
Tyra Banks vs. Netflix
                          Videos Show What 'ANTM' Doc Left Out!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 22, 2026
                            2:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Tyra Banks believes she finally has the receipts to clear her name after getting dragged in Netflix's "America's Next Top Model" docuseries ... pointing to a couple of comparison videos she says show her words were twisted.
      
    
            In Tyra's latest filing, obtained by TMZ, Tyra uses the videos to fight Netflix's attempt to dismiss her defamation lawsuit.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The first video centers on former contestant Shandi Sullivan. After Shandi describes an alleged sexual assault in the documentary, Tyra is asked, "You remember the story with Shandi?"
      
    
            Episode 1 leaves viewers with Tyra saying "Um" before cutting to black -- making it appear as if she was unable to say whether she remembered the alleged assault on a contestant on the show.
      

            But Tyra says footage from Episode 2 shows Tyra actually nodded and answered, "Um ... I do remember her story." Her attorneys put it bluntly: "The nod was not cut off. It was cut out."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The second video compares the docuseries with Tyra's original 2004 coffee conversation with Shandi.
      
    
            According to Tyra, the documentary makes it look like Tyra brought up cheating with producers "in her ear," but the original footage shows Shandi introduced the subject by asking whether Tyra had ever cheated or been cheated on.
      
    
            Tyra claims the conversation was reordered to make her look like she raised the topic and got Shandi to confess to cheating on camera.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Tyra faced major backlash over the documentary, including mockery from original 'ANTM' winner Adrianne Curry.
      
    
            Tyra says the videos prove her lawsuit is not about wanting more airtime or a better edit -- it's about editing she insists changed the meaning of what she actually said.
      
    
            Netflix has denied wrongdoing and says the filmmakers fairly presented Tyra's perspective, and a hearing on its motion to dismiss is scheduled for October 30.
      
    
            Stay tuned ...
